title: The fit sample
brief:
Write a complete workplace story for adult readers about a small company that makes cushion covers. Bea cuts fabric, Rami handles orders, and the owner leaves them to prepare a sample for a furniture shop's buyer by Thursday afternoon. The buyer's old cushion was restuffed last winter, and its measurements differ from the paper pattern by two centimeters across the widest point. The company has enough of the chosen fabric for two samples. Set the story over three workdays. Convey the work through concrete actions and conversations, and make the sample handoff a test of how Bea and Rami share responsibility.

Aim for 1,200 to 1,800 words. Return the complete original work directly in your answer. Do not sign or identify yourself. Do not use tools.

8dc237a5bd13dea1.text:
On Tuesday morning, before she left for the mill, Judith set a faded green cushion on Bea’s cutting table. It had a shallow hollow along one edge where somebody had sat with one leg tucked under them.

“Marsh Furniture,” she said. “Their buyer will be here Thursday at three. She wants a sample for the low walnut chair. Between you, can you see it through?”

Bea put down her shears. Rami came out from behind the plywood partition that made the far end of the room an office.

“Who signs for it?” he asked.

“You do,” Judith said, pulling on her coat. “Either of you knows how to spell our name.”

There were four people at Vale Covers when everybody was in. That week the machinist was home with a boy who had chickenpox. Bea could sew well enough to stand in for her. Rami could run the steam iron, pack a carton so its corners stayed square, and tell you which of their customers would take a call before lunch.

He opened the order folder. Inside lay a brown paper pattern, a photograph of the chair and a note in the buyer’s hand. *Our showroom cushion. Restuffed last winter. Please return.*

Bea unzipped the old cover. A cloud of white fibres clung to her sleeve. She eased out the pad, turned the cover inside out and laid the upper panel flat. Across its widest point, from stitch line to stitch line, it measured fifty-four centimetres. The paper pattern had the stitching line drawn in blue pencil. Fifty-two.

“Which one did you quote?” she asked.

“The chair in the photograph.”

“You could fit anything to a photograph.”

“I quoted a price, Bea. Nobody asked me to fit it.”

The chosen cloth was an oat-coloured wool with a narrow rust stripe. She unrolled it across the table. Allowing for the stripes to meet at the front corners, there was enough for two complete samples. Then they would be down to pieces fit for covering buttons.

Rami reached for his phone. The buyer, Helen Marsh, was on the shop floor. He left a message asking which measurement she wanted them to use.

“Say why,” Bea said as he was about to hang up.

He put the phone back to his ear. “Your old cover measures two centimetres wider than the pattern. We’d like to know which one fits the chairs you’re selling.”

Bea traced the paper onto card. She marked the centre of the front curve with a notch, then made a second card template from the old top, working her way round its edge with pins. At four, the buyer still hadn’t called. Rami found Bea sliding weights onto the wool.

“You’re cutting the small one?”

“I’m cutting the one thing that’s the same on both.”

She held up a strip for the back where the zip would go. On the cutting table lay two little piles of rust-coloured thread from the selvedge. The rest of the cloth was whole.

On Wednesday, Helen rang while Bea was feeding the zip strip under the machine foot. Rami brought the cordless phone across and put it on speaker.

“The paper came from our frame maker,” Helen said. “The old cushion is the one people try in the shop. They like how it sits. I thought the upholsterer just put fresh filling in.”

“Have you got another of the chairs there?” Bea asked.

“Six in boxes. I can have one put together for tomorrow.”

“Bring it along if you can.”

There was a little silence. “I drive a Polo.”

“Back legs come off,” Rami said. He had enlarged the photograph on his monitor. “There are bolts underneath. I’ll come and collect it at lunch.”

After the call Bea drew a line with her thumbnail through the nap of the wool.

“What did you promise her?” she asked.

“A chair ride. It’s half a mile.”

“On the order. What have we said this cover will do?”

He fetched the original email. He had written, *We can reproduce your showroom cushion for the new frames.* He had been pleased with the economy of that sentence when he wrote it. Reading it aloud took longer than he remembered.

Bea pulled the photograph close. “Better bring the seat pad that comes with the new frame, too.”

At half past one he carried the chair in sideways, then went back downstairs for the new pad and a parking ticket. The chair arms curled inwards at the front. Bea laid the two templates on the seat in turn. The small one cleared the arms. The larger one caught, but card couldn’t tell them what wool and a full pad would do.

“Make both,” Rami said.

“And if I put a needle through the wrong place on the second one?”

He looked at the remaining cloth. In the office he kept a margin on every delivery date, an extra afternoon for a failed collection or a street somebody had dug up. He had just spent hers.

“What would you do first?” he asked.

“Make the paper one. Put it on their new pad. Then we’ll know what we’re using the last piece for.”

He moved the chair into the good light and stripped the plastic off the pad. While Bea sewed, he measured the distance between the arms at three places and wrote the figures on the back of the parking ticket.

By four they had the first cover zipped. The stripe ran straight from the back to the front lip. On the new pad it sat neatly between the arms. Rami lowered himself into the chair. When he stood, the cushion rose with him for a moment, then dropped back into place.

Bea tried the old pad in it. She got the zip halfway before the teeth spread behind the slider. She swore and worked them free.

“We can give her a good fit on the stock chair,” she said. “Or we can make her old cushion look new.”

Rami sat on the old pad in its green cover. He shifted his weight and ran a hand under his thigh. “This is the one I’d buy.”

“So would I.”

He took the order sheet from its plastic sleeve. Under his original description he wrote down what they had tried, including the zip. Then he drew two empty boxes for Helen to choose between.

On Thursday morning Bea cut the larger cover. At the front curve she eased the cloth under the foot a stitch at a time. Rami stood at the iron, pressing the boxing seams open over a little wooden block. She had shown him how much steam the wool could take. By eleven he could feel through the handle when the seam had settled.

The larger cover went over the old pad with room for two fingers behind the slider. In the new chair its front corners pressed against the arms. After Rami sat in it, the right corner stayed folded under. Bea reached to pull it straight.

“Leave it,” he said. “She’ll want to see where it catches.”

Helen arrived at three carrying a shopping bag for her old cushion. She took off her coat, sat in the chair and got up. She saw the turned corner. Then she tried the smaller sample on the new pad. She pressed the seat with the heel of her hand.

“Which one am I taking back?” she asked.

Rami had the form ready on his clipboard. Bea could see his thumb resting between the boxes.

“The small one goes on the chair you’ll deliver,” he said. “I told you we could reproduce the showroom cushion for those frames. I should have asked about the pads before I wrote that.”

Helen looked at Bea. “Could you shave a bit off here?” She pinched the bigger cover at the corner.

“I could bring the seam in,” Bea said. “Your old pad would still be pushing against it. I’d send the small cover out with the new pad, and I’d let customers sit on that before they order.”

Helen sat down again. This time she slipped off her shoes and drew one leg up. The old green cushion lay on the table beside her, its hollow exactly the shape of her heel.

“My brother says I’ve been selling people my chair for years,” she said. She stayed there another moment. “All right. Small cover, new pad. I’ll put it on the floor on Saturday.”

Rami marked the box. When he offered Bea the pen, she read the sentence above it. *Customer selected pattern size.*

“Give me another line,” she said.

He turned the clipboard sideways to make room. She added, *Tried on new Marsh pad in walnut frame, with buyer present.* She signed beside the measurement. Rami signed beside the delivery description and gave Helen the top copy.

Together they put the green cover back on the old pad. Helen took it in her shopping bag, and Rami carried the sample and the chair down to her car. When he came back, Bea was unpicking the paper tag from the larger sample. It still said *Marsh order* in his handwriting.

“What do we call this one?” she asked.

He thought about the next person who might open the cupboard looking for a pattern. “Showroom pad, fifty-four. Catches at right arm.”

She wrote it out. He held the tag flat while she fastened it through the zip pull.

57a82305411de2b8.text:
On Tuesday morning, Helen laid a brown paper pattern on Bea’s cutting table and set an armchair cushion on top of it. The cushion had come in a bin bag with the name of a furniture shop written on masking tape.

“Thursday at two,” Helen said. “Nina’s bringing the chair. She wants to see a cover on it before she decides about an order.”

“Which cloth?” Bea asked.

“The green.”

Bea looked at the bolt under the table. It had arrived on Friday with a note from the mill tucked into the end. The next dye lot was due in six weeks.

“Enough for two,” she said.

“Then you’ve got two.” Helen fished her van keys out of her apron. She was going to clear her sister’s flat and had taken three days off. A man was coming for the washing machine at ten. “Rami’s got the email. Put the sample on my account.”

Rami came through from the office carrying two mugs and the printed email. He set Bea’s mug on the windowsill, where she liked it, and read out the line he had underlined. “‘Please use our existing Bracken pattern. I’ve sent the cushion from the floor chair so you can show it made up.’”

Bea took the cushion out of its bag. Its cover was shiny along the front edge, and the zip pull had been replaced with a loop of fishing line. She laid the paper flat beside it and measured between the seam lines at the broadest point. Fifty-eight centimeters. On the cushion, seam to seam, she got sixty. She stood two square blocks against the sides and measured between those. Sixty again.

Rami held down the curling corner of the pattern. “Would it go in at fifty-eight?”

“Probably. Sit on that end a minute.”

He sat. The front edge swelled out between his knees and the zip gave a small clicking sound.

“Get up,” Bea said.

She undid the zip. Inside was a thick piece of foam wrapped in white batting. The batting had been folded back on itself at both sides, with the folds held by loose stitches. A scrap of blue thread hung from one of them.

Rami phoned the shop. Nina was out, but the man who answered remembered taking the cushion to an upholsterer last winter. Customers had been sinking into the chair and feeling the rail underneath. He thought the upholsterer had kept the old cover and put everything else in the skip.

“Did you do the others?” Rami asked.

“Which others?”

“The other Brackens.”

“Oh,” the man said. “We’ve got loads.”

Rami left a message for Nina. At eleven he sent her an email with the two measurements in it. Bea spread the green cloth face up on the table. The weave looked darker when she ran her hand toward the bolt. She turned one of the paper pieces through half a circle, watched it change color against its neighbor, and turned it back. With a single direction for the pieces she could get two covers, provided she cut the zip panels from the narrow strip beside the tops.

At half past three Rami came back with the email open on his phone.

“She’s buying at an auction. Her assistant says she’ll ring when she gets out.”

Bea had a set of six cream covers due for collection in the morning. She could finish those now and keep Wednesday for the green.

“If we cut one to the paper first,” Rami said, “we can still do the other after she rings.”

“You want me to cut it?”

“I want to have something to show her.”

“So do I.” Bea slid the weights off the green cloth. “I’ll start in the morning.”

On Wednesday, Bea ran the steel rule down the paper and marked the cloth with chalk. Rami watched from the doorway until she lifted the shears.

“Can you put it on the job sheet?” she said.

“What am I putting?”

“Paper pattern, fifty-eight. Then we’ll know what’s in the bag when we do the next one.”

He went back to the office. Before Bea finished cutting the top, he returned with a job sheet on a clipboard. He had written *Cut to existing pattern as requested*. Below that, in the space for special instructions, he had entered both measurements and the time he’d called the shop.

They got the first cover onto the cushion just before lunch. Bea held the foam bent while Rami worked the zip around the corner. The teeth closed, and a diagonal crease appeared on each side of the front. Bea pushed the cushion down with both palms. When she let go, the creases came back.

Rami took a photograph.

“From the side as well,” Bea said.

Nina rang at twelve forty. Rami put her on speaker and set the phone on a cone of thread so they could both hear.

“The shop floor is what I’ve got to get right first,” Nina said. “That chair’s in the window. The owner wants a price for twelve while I’m there.”

“Twelve covers?” Rami asked.

“Twelve chairs’ worth. We’ve been buying them back from customers for years. We put fresh covers on and sell them again.”

“Have you got the cushions together anywhere?”

“Some are in the warehouse. Two are at the upholsterer’s now.”

Bea looked at the strained corners of the green cover. “Will the upholsterer be making those two up to a size you give him?”

There was a pause. Through the phone they heard a metal drawer shut.

“I can ask him,” Nina said. “Can I see the green on the chair tomorrow?”

Bea said she could.

When the call ended, Rami reached for the clipboard. “Sixty for the floor chair.”

“Come hold this down first.”

They took the green cover off. Bea laid a sheet of fresh paper over the old pattern, traced the back and marked the midpoint of the front. She brought the sides out a centimeter each where the cushion was widest, then drew the curves back toward the old corners. Rami kept his fingers on the paper as she moved the rule.

“What goes on this one?” he asked.

“Floor cushion, sixty. Put the date on it.”

He moved his thumb and she drew through the place where it had been.

Bea finished the second cover on Thursday at eleven twenty. The new zip ran shut with room for her fingertip beneath the pull. She set the cushion on the packing bench and went to wash the chalk off her hands. When she came back, Rami was smoothing the loose first cover on a sheet of tissue.

“Do you want both out?” he asked.

“Yes,” Bea said. “Leave that one flat till she’s seen the other.”

Nina arrived at ten to two with the Bracken chair in the back of her estate car. Rami helped carry it in. One of its front feet had lost a felt pad and it rocked on the concrete, so he folded a piece of card and wedged it underneath. Bea lowered the cushion into the frame. The green front edge sat just above the rail.

Nina took off her coat and sat. She leaned over one arm, then the other, and ran her fingers down the side of the cushion to where it met the wood.

“Yes,” she said. “I can put that in the window.”

Rami brought the sample receipt over. Nina picked up his pen. “If I sign here, can you get the twelve underway? Graham wants them for the spring floor change. If I come back with one cover and a date for twelve, I can get him to release the money today.”

Rami had printed the quantity of twelve on the quotation that morning. Bea had seen it by the office printer and assumed he’d put a condition next to it. From where she stood she could see the blank space under the price.

“That price is for twelve made to one pattern,” Rami said. “I put it together before we knew where all the cushions were.”

Nina kept the pen in her hand. “Can I tell him it’ll be this pattern?”

Bea lifted the cushion from the chair and carried it to the bench. “I can show you what happens with the other one.”

She pulled the sixty-centimeter cover halfway off, then slid the first cover over the front corners. She got as far as closing the zip halfway before the two creases formed. Nina came to the bench and put her palm on one. It sprang up when she took her hand away.

“I made that one from the paper you sent,” Bea said. “The one you sat on is drawn from this cushion. I’d like to put a tape on one of the warehouse cushions before I cut the batch.”

Nina looked down at the cover. “Graham will ask why I sent you a pattern.”

“Tell him we used it,” Rami said. He took back the quotation and drew a line beneath the price. “I’ll write what the price covers. If you can get us into the warehouse Monday, we can measure what’s there and speak to the upholsterer while we’re with you.”

Bea had planned to spend Monday on kitchen seat pads. She counted the pieces she could cut before leaving on Friday.

“Before ten,” she said. “I can come before ten.”

Nina checked her phone. “I open up at eight.”

Rami wrote eight thirty on his copy. On the sample receipt he entered one green cover, fitted to the shop-floor cushion. He passed it to Bea, who added sixty centimeters and signed beside the measurement. Rami signed underneath and gave Nina the pen.

They carried the chair out together. Nina held the car door while Rami guided the back legs past the latch. Bea brought the cushion last, wrapped in the clean tissue Rami had laid out that morning. Nina cleared a space for it beside her coat. Before she shut the door she peeled back the tissue and pressed the green fabric once with the flat of her hand.

Inside, Rami picked up the first cover from the packing bench.

“Where do you want this?”

“On the shelf with both patterns. We’ll take it Monday.”

He folded it along the side seams. Bea rolled the two sheets of paper around the same cardboard tube, leaving enough of each edge showing to read the measurements.
